<reason>Both sides argued the motion as written and executed the Q&A format properly, but B built the tighter structural case. B's key move—turning A's own "captive demand" theory against it by noting that if high rates were pure extractive surplus, issuers would simply keep lending to desperate borrowers at a lower cap rather than cut them off, so the motion's own "even if" clause implicitly concedes the rates were closer to actuarial necessity—was never squarely answered by A, who mostly reasserted that CON hadn't "proven" its claim rather than rebutting the logic. B's pressure questions also extracted a real concession: A admitted that a cap cannot separate "good-use" borrowers (who'd pay down debt) from "bad-use" borrowers (who'd stall), and would still affirm even when the former group is cut off entirely. That concession undercuts A's founding dichotomy that what's lost is merely a "debt trap," not real credit access, and A's attempted recovery (status quo also lumps borrowers together) addresses sorting precision but not the magnitude difference between "pay somewhat more" and "denied entirely." A's compound-interest mechanism is real and vivid, but it proves high rates are costly, not that cutting access nets out better for the excluded population—the actual crux the motion demands be confronted. B's closing line crystallizing "a costly card can still keep a job; an admitted lockout cannot" was the cleaner, more decisive frame. A's opening was also clipped before its final weighing sentence, a minor execution cost.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's [B2.4]/[B4.1] point—that if rates were pure captive-demand surplus, issuers would keep serving desperate borrowers at the lower cap, so the motion's "even if" cutoff itself is evidence the price was closer to necessary—combined with the concession B extracted in Pressure Questions that A still affirms even when good-use borrowers are cut alongside bad-use ones.</best_rebuttal>
